page.title: Money & Health: Budgets, Debt and Health Costs | WealthLanding
page.description: Guides and calculators for everyday money decisions: paychecks, budgets, debt payoff, health insurance choices, HSAs and legitimate ways to spend less.
intro: Day-to-day money decisions add up: what you keep from each paycheck, how fast debt disappears, and what you pay for health coverage. This section collects WealthLanding's guides and calculators on those decisions, with the rules and the math explained plainly.

If you are choosing a health plan during open enrollment, start with the plan comparison tool. If debt is the pressure point, start with the payoff calculator. Every tool page explains its assumptions and walks through a worked example.

questions.q: Which health plan should I pick?
questions.a: Compare the total yearly cost, not just the premium. Premiums are fixed, while deductibles and coinsurance depend on how much care you use. The comparison tool shows the spending level where each plan becomes the cheaper choice.

questions.q: How do I get out of debt faster?
questions.a: List every balance with its rate and minimum payment. Paying the highest rate first (avalanche) costs the least interest; paying the smallest balance first (snowball) brings earlier wins. Either works if the extra payment keeps going.

questions.q: How can I spend less without giving up what matters?
questions.a: The Deal Finder collects legitimate discounts on flights, hotels, rental cars, theme parks, museums and events, and the case study shows the savings on one family trip.

questions.q: Is my family protected if something happens?
questions.a: Insurance replaces income or covers costs you could not absorb. Check what your employer already provides before buying more.

page.title: Real Estate: Rent vs Buy, Buying, Renting and Downsizing | WealthLanding
page.description: After-tax rent vs buy, how much house you can sustain, buying and renting checklists, investment property realities, and downsizing at 45–65 — with IRS and CFPB primary sources.
page.h1: Housing decisions, connected end to end
intro: A home is often both the largest purchase and the largest single asset a household owns. These guides walk the decision tree: rent versus buy on an after-tax basis, how much house a budget can sustain, how to buy or rent on purpose, what changes when the property is an investment, and how to downsize or relocate in the 45–65 years.
There is no universal winner. Every guide labels assumptions, links official IRS and CFPB sources for tax and mortgage rules, and points to the next step that fits your situation.

questions.a: Compare equal cash flows and after-tax terminal wealth. Factor investment capital gains, the main-home sale exclusion if you qualify ($250,000 / $500,000), amortization, leverage, and labeled home-price scenarios — not a guaranteed rise.

questions.q: How much house can I afford?
questions.a: Separate lender approval from a sustainable all-in payment (PITI, HOA, PMI, maintenance, reserves). Stress-test income drops and retirement contributions, especially at 45–65.

questions.q: What should I check when buying a primary home?
questions.a: Compare Loan Estimates and the Closing Disclosure, keep key contingencies, and verify inspections, title, flood risk, insurance, taxes and HOA reserves before you waive protections.

Net out selling costs and confirm IRS main-home exclusion eligibility, then price the next home or rental against healthcare access, taxes and retirement cash needs. Renting first in a new area reduces costly mistakes.

questions.q: Is a rental property a good investment?
questions.a: Underwrite cash flow after vacancy, repairs, capex and debt service. Cap rate is not a personal return promise. Read IRS Publications 527 and 925 for depreciation and passive-loss themes, and do not assume the main-home exclusion applies.

questions.q: What is the housing market doing?
questions.a: Headline numbers can point in opposite directions. Use FHFA price data and articles that explain what each series measures.

page.title: Travel & Rewards: Loyalty Programs, Status and Card Perks | WealthLanding
page.description: How airline and hotel loyalty programs work, whether elite status is worth it, and which credit card to use for each purchase, with calculators and real trip case studies.
page.h1: Points, status and card perks that fit how you travel
intro: Loyalty programs and credit card perks can be worth real money, but only when they match how you actually travel. These guides explain how airline and hotel programs award status, what elite benefits do and don't cover, and how to route everyday spending to the right card.
If you plan to travel more as work winds down, the case studies show how program rules played out on real trips, including what happened when plans went wrong.

questions.q: Which airline program fits my home airport?
questions.a: Status is most useful with the airline that flies the most routes from where you live. The airline guides compare how each program earns and spends miles and which cities each one serves best.
Compare what you would spend to earn status with the benefits you would actually use, such as upgrades, free checked bags and same-day changes.

questions.q: Which hotel program should I focus on?
questions.a: Pick the chain with hotels where you travel most, then compare how quickly each program's nights and points turn into free stays.

questions.q: Which card should I use for each purchase?
questions.a: The best card depends on the category of spending and on the protections you need, not only on the points rate.

questions.q: How do I pay less for the trip itself?
questions.a: Flexible dates, the right booking channel and memberships you already hold often matter more than points.
